Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- The bodies of young elephants covered in the brown dirt of dried-up wells tell a heartrending story. A baby elephant in the Gourma region of central Mali had been trapped in a well for three days. Reaching desperately for drops of water, they had lowered their trunks, toppled in, remained trapped and died in Mali's scorching heat. The "last desert elephants in West Africa" have "adapted to survive in the harsh conditions" they face, Save the Elephants said Monday. But now, the group says, conditions have gone from bad to worse, and they are living "on the margin of what is ecologically viable." Save the Elephants distributed new pictures Monday that depict the devastating drought and the struggle for survival in Mali, one of the poorest nations in the world. "Six elephants have already been found dead," the group wrote in a news release accompanying the photos. "Four others, including three calves, were recently extracted from a shallow well into which they had fallen when searching for water. Only the largest survived." The youngest are in the most danger, since their smaller trunks can't reach deep into the few remaining wells, the group said. The worst drought in 26 years is threatening the existence of the "last desert elephants in West Africa," the northernmost herds in the continent, Save the Elephants said. The animals, now numbering only about 350 to 450, have been called "the last elephants of Timbuktu," said Jake Wall, a scientist with Save the Elephants. But they're south of Timbuktu, Wall told CNN in a phone interview from Bamako, Mali. "We tend to refer to them as 'the last Sahelian elephants.' "  See a map of Mali » . Each year, the elephants trek farther on the fringes of the Sahara to find water. They have the longest migration route of any in the continent, traveling "in a counterclockwise circle" of about 700 kilometers (435 miles), Save the Elephants said. The images are signs of the crisis gripping the northwest African nation. The U.N. Development Programme ranks Mali near the bottom of its Human Development Index. It cites a 56 percent poverty rate in the country, with nearly a third of the population unlikely to live past age 40, and an illiteracy rate of 77 percent. The World Food Programme says the majority of infant deaths in Mali are due to malnutrition. The drought, combined with soaring temperatures, has also led to deaths of cattle, Save the Elephants said. "The stench of rotting corpses fills the air, and what little water remains is putrid and undrinkable by all standards." In areas where the elephants live and search for water, "the normal peaceful coexistence between the elephants and herdsmen is starting to break down and giving way to conflict over access to water," Wall said. There is some hope for the weeks and months ahead. "We're hoping the rains start in June, and that will allow the elephants to start drinking out of shallow ponds until the really heavy rains begin" in July or August, Wall said. But "urgent action" is needed in the interim "to secure water for the elephants," Wall's group said in its news release. Save the Elephants, which focuses on helping elephant populations worldwide, said it has partnered with a foundation and the Mali government in its fundraising appeal.

(CNN) — The sight of young elephants’ bodies, coated with the brown dust from dried wells, reveals a deeply tragic situation.

In Mali’s central Gourma region, one elephant calf had been stuck in a well for three days. Searching desperately for even small amounts of water, the elephants had stretched their trunks downward, lost their footing, fallen in, become unable to escape, and died under Mali’s intense heat.

Save the Elephants said Monday that the animals known as the “last desert elephants in West Africa” have learned to endure the severe environment around them. But the organization warned that circumstances have deteriorated sharply, leaving the elephants living at the very edge of what the ecosystem can support.

On Monday, Save the Elephants released new photographs showing the severe drought and the fight to stay alive in Mali, one of the world’s poorest countries.

“Six elephants have already been found dead,” the organization said in a news release issued with the images. It added that four more elephants, among them three calves, had recently been pulled from a shallow well after falling in while trying to find water. Of those four, only the biggest animal survived.

According to the group, the youngest elephants face the greatest risk because their shorter trunks cannot reach far enough down into the few wells that still contain water.

Save the Elephants said the worst drought in 26 years is endangering the survival of the “last desert elephants in West Africa,” which are the continent’s northernmost elephant herds.

Jake Wall, a scientist with Save the Elephants, said the population now consists of only about 350 to 450 animals. They have sometimes been described as “the last elephants of Timbuktu,” he said. However, Wall told CNN by phone from Bamako, Mali, that the elephants actually live south of Timbuktu. “We tend to refer to them as ‘the last Sahelian elephants,’” he said.

Each year, the elephants travel along the edge of the Sahara in search of water. Save the Elephants said they follow the longest migration route of any elephants on the continent, moving in “a counterclockwise circle” that covers roughly 700 kilometers, or 435 miles.

The photographs reflect the broader emergency affecting the northwest African country. The U.N. Development Programme places Mali close to the bottom of its Human Development Index. It reports that 56 percent of Mali’s population lives in poverty, nearly one-third of people are unlikely to live beyond age 40, and 77 percent of the population is illiterate.

The World Food Programme says most infant deaths in Mali are caused by malnutrition.

Save the Elephants said the drought, along with extremely high temperatures, has also killed cattle. “The stench of rotting corpses fills the air, and what little water remains is putrid and undrinkable by all standards,” the group said.

Wall said that in the places where the elephants live and look for water, “the normal peaceful coexistence between the elephants and herdsmen is starting to break down and giving way to conflict over access to water.”

There is still some possibility of relief in the coming weeks and months. Wall said, “We’re hoping the rains start in June, and that will allow the elephants to start drinking out of shallow ponds until the really heavy rains begin” in July or August.

Until then, Save the Elephants said in its release that “urgent action” is necessary “to secure water for the elephants.”

The organization, which works to protect elephant populations around the world, said it has joined with a foundation and Mali’s government in an effort to raise funds.

But conservationists say traditional migration routes have become increasingly difficult to navigate because of drought, human settlement, insecurity and competition for scarce resources.

Save the Elephants warned that without urgent action to secure water points, protect migration corridors and reduce conflict between elephants and communities, the herd could face collapse.

“These elephants have survived in one of the toughest environments on Earth,” the organization said in its warning. “But the loss of water is pushing them beyond their limits.”

**Drought threatens Mali’s last Sahelian elephants as people and wildlife compete for shrinking water**

*GOURMA, Mali —* The last surviving herd of Sahelian elephants in Mali is facing a deepening drought emergency, conservationists warn, as water holes dry up across the country’s conflict-hit central and northern regions and desperate communities struggle with the same shortage.

The elephants, often described as the world’s northernmost and most desert-adapted elephants, roam the Gourma region south of the Niger River, moving through a vast seasonal migration circuit across scrubland, dunes and temporary wetlands. Their survival depends on finding scattered water and grazing across an area that can span tens of thousands of square kilometres.

Save the Elephants scientist **Jake Wall**, who has studied elephant movements using satellite tracking, said the crisis is becoming increasingly acute.

> “These elephants are living on the edge of what is possible for the species,” Wall said. “Their movements are driven by water, and when the water points fail, the risk to the herd rises dramatically.”

The Gourma elephants typically follow an annual migration pattern tied to rainfall. During the wet season, they move north and east into remote pastures where seasonal vegetation appears after the rains. As the dry season tightens, they return toward more reliable water sources, including areas around the Gourma’s remaining lakes and ponds. Conservationists say the route can cover several hundred kilometres and is one of the longest known elephant migrations in Africa.

But that ancient pattern is being disrupted. Poor rains, hotter temperatures and the degradation of grazing land have reduced the availability of water across the elephants’ range. In some places, wells and ponds that once supported both wildlife and herders are now drying earlier in the year. The result is a dangerous convergence: elephants, livestock and people are being pushed toward the same shrinking water points.

> “When elephants are forced to crowd around the last available water, they become more vulnerable — to hunger, to conflict with people, and to poaching,” Wall said. “Keeping their migration corridors open is essential.”

The herd is believed to number only a few hundred animals at most, making every loss significant. Mali’s elephants have survived harsh desert conditions for generations, but conservationists say drought now combines with insecurity, habitat loss and human pressure in ways that threaten the population’s long-term future.

The humanitarian backdrop is severe. Mali has endured years of armed conflict involving state forces, separatist groups and Islamist militants, particularly in central and northern regions. The violence has displaced communities, disrupted markets, limited access for aid groups and weakened local governance. At the same time, climate shocks have worsened food insecurity across the Sahel, where pastoralists and farmers are already struggling with erratic rainfall, rising food prices and loss of livestock.

In areas used by the elephants, many families depend on cattle, goats and sheep, meaning water scarcity quickly becomes a survival issue. Herders may drive animals deeper into elephant habitat in search of pasture, while farmers cultivate land closer to migration routes. That increases the chance of crop damage, confrontations and retaliatory killings.

Local conservation initiatives have previously shown that coexistence is possible. Community patrols, information networks and protection of key water points have helped reduce poaching and guide herders away from the most sensitive elephant areas. However, insecurity has made field operations more difficult, and drought is testing the limits of these efforts.

Conservation groups are calling for urgent action to protect critical water sources, preserve migration corridors and support local communities so that people are not forced into direct competition with elephants. Measures could include repairing wells for villages and livestock, monitoring elephant movements, preventing illegal killing, and coordinating humanitarian relief with conservation planning.

Wall said the future of the herd depends on treating the crisis as both an environmental and human emergency.

> “You cannot separate the elephants’ survival from the wellbeing of the people who share this landscape,” he said. “If communities have water, security and support, the elephants have a chance too.”

The Gourma elephants are among the last symbols of a wilder Sahel — animals that have adapted to extreme heat, long-distance travel and scarce resources. But conservationists warn that adaptation has limits. If drought intensifies and water sources continue to vanish, Mali could lose one of its most extraordinary natural populations.

For now, the herd continues to move, following routes passed down over generations. Whether those routes will still lead to water in the years ahead is the question now confronting Mali, conservationists and humanitarian agencies alike.

## Young elephants found dead in wells as drought and conflict threaten Mali’s last herd

Young elephants have been found dead in deep wells in central Mali, a grim sign of the growing struggle for water in one of the world’s harshest environments and a warning that the country’s last remaining elephants are under mounting threat.

Conservationists say the deaths are linked to worsening drought, expanding human hardship and rising competition over scarce water sources across the Sahel. Mali’s surviving elephants — estimated at just 350 to 450 animals — are among the last desert-adapted elephants on Earth, known for making one of the longest seasonal migrations of any elephant population as they search for water and grazing land.

But that ancient migration route is becoming increasingly dangerous.

As ponds dry earlier and rains become more unpredictable, elephants are being pushed closer to villages, livestock and man-made wells. Young elephants, desperate for water or following adults into unfamiliar areas, can fall into the steep, narrow shafts and become trapped. In some cases, they die before rescuers can reach them.

The crisis is not only environmental. Poverty has deepened across parts of central Mali, where many families depend on livestock and small-scale farming. As water becomes harder to find, people dig more wells and guard access to them more closely. Elephants, which can drink large quantities and damage water points, are sometimes seen as competitors rather than protected animals.

That tension is being worsened by insecurity. Armed conflict and instability across central and northern Mali have disrupted conservation work, limited patrols and made it harder for local authorities and wildlife groups to monitor elephant movements or respond quickly when animals are in danger. Communities already facing violence, displacement and food shortages often have little capacity to cope with crop damage or broken wells caused by elephants.

Mali’s elephants live mainly in the Gourma region, moving across a vast landscape between seasonal water sources. Unlike many elephant populations, they have adapted to semi-arid conditions, traveling long distances through scrubland and desert-edge terrain. Their survival depends on access to a chain of water points — a chain now increasingly broken by drought, human pressure and insecurity.

Experts warn that the deaths of young elephants are especially concerning because the population is already small. Losing calves and juveniles weakens the herd’s ability to recover and increases the risk of long-term decline. With only a few hundred animals left, even a limited number of deaths can have serious consequences.

Local communities are central to any solution. Conservation groups have called for better protection of wells, emergency response teams to rescue trapped animals, and support for herders and farmers who share land with elephants. Measures such as covering dangerous wells, creating wildlife-friendly water access points and compensating communities for damage could reduce conflict.

But those efforts require stability and funding — both difficult to secure in a region grappling with climate stress and armed violence.

For Mali’s last elephants, the search for water has always defined survival. Now, as drought tightens its grip and people and animals are forced into closer competition, that search is becoming deadly.

**BREAKING NEWS: Photos show Mali’s “last elephants of Timbuktu” fighting for water as calves die in worsening crisis**

*By [Reporter Name]*

Save the Elephants has released stark new photographs of Mali’s famed “last elephants of Timbuktu,” showing exhausted animals clustered around dwindling water sources in the country’s Sahelian north — a visual warning, conservationists say, that one of the world’s most extraordinary elephant populations is running out of time.

The images, taken in the Gourma region south of Timbuktu, capture elephants moving across an increasingly dry and insecure landscape in search of water and forage. Conservationists say calves are among the first victims of the crisis, with young elephants dying as herds are forced to travel farther, wait longer, and compete harder for access to shrinking water points.

Save the Elephants said the photographs are intended to draw urgent attention to the plight of Mali’s desert-adapted elephants, often described as the last remaining elephants of Timbuktu. The animals are famous for undertaking one of the longest migrations of any elephant population, moving across hundreds of kilometers of harsh Sahel terrain to track seasonal rains, wetlands and pasture.

But that ancient survival strategy is now under severe pressure.

Years of drought, expanding human use of land and water, insecurity, and the breakdown of conservation support in parts of central and northern Mali have left the elephants increasingly vulnerable. Waterholes that once sustained herds during the dry season are becoming unreliable. In some places, elephants are forced toward human settlements, raising the risk of conflict with communities already facing hardship.

Conservationists warn that without immediate intervention, Mali’s remaining elephants could suffer further calf losses — a devastating blow for a population already considered fragile.

“These elephants are living on the edge,” campaigners said in releasing the photographs, stressing that the animals need emergency support to survive the dry season. “If water disappears, calves die first. The loss of young elephants threatens the future of the entire herd.”

The crisis is not only ecological. Mali’s elephants live in a region affected by armed conflict, displacement and limited state access, complicating efforts to monitor the animals, repair water infrastructure, support local communities and protect migration routes. Conservation groups say the situation requires both urgent fundraising and renewed government action.

Immediate priorities include maintaining and restoring critical water points, supporting local guardians and community-based protection teams, improving monitoring of the herds, and reducing conflict between elephants and people. Conservationists are also calling for stronger coordination between Mali’s authorities, local communities and international partners to keep the elephants’ migration corridor open.

The elephants of the Gourma have long been a symbol of resilience. Unlike forest and savanna elephants in more stable habitats, Mali’s desert elephants have survived for generations by following an intricate circular migration across semi-arid lands near Timbuktu, Gao and the wider Gourma zone. Their survival depends on access to seasonal water and vegetation — resources now under increasing strain.

The deaths of calves are particularly alarming because elephant populations recover slowly. Females have long pregnancies and calves require years of care. Even a small rise in calf mortality can have lasting consequences, especially in an isolated population with limited room to rebound.

Save the Elephants’ appeal is expected to focus on emergency funding to help keep water available through the most dangerous months, while pressing for longer-term protection of habitat and migration routes. Conservationists say that without decisive action, the world could lose one of its most remarkable elephant populations — not through a single catastrophic event, but through a slow collapse driven by thirst, insecurity and neglect.

For Mali, the stakes are cultural as well as environmental. The “elephants of Timbuktu” are among the country’s most iconic wild animals, deeply tied to the landscape and history of the Sahel. Their disappearance would mark the loss of a rare desert-adapted population and a powerful symbol of survival in one of the world’s toughest environments.

As the new photographs circulate, conservationists are urging donors, governments and international agencies to act quickly.

The message is simple: Mali’s last elephants need water now — and protection for the future.

**Mali’s worst drought in 26 years threatens West Africa’s last desert elephants**

**BAMAKO, Mali (CNN)** — The worst drought to hit Mali in 26 years is threatening one of West Africa’s rarest wildlife populations: the region’s last desert elephants, whose survival depends on an annual migration of roughly 700 kilometers across the country’s arid north.

Conservationists say shrinking water sources and disappearing vegetation are putting new pressure on the elephants, which roam the Gourma region near the edge of the Sahara. The animals are known for one of the longest elephant migrations in the world, traveling vast distances between seasonal lakes and pastures in search of food and water.

But this year, those routes have become increasingly fragile. Failed rains have dried ponds earlier than usual, reduced grazing land and intensified competition between wildlife, livestock and communities already struggling with food insecurity.

The drought is also worsening a humanitarian crisis in Mali, where malnutrition remains a major concern, particularly among children. Aid groups have warned that poor harvests, conflict and high food prices are leaving families with fewer ways to cope.

For the elephants, the stakes are high. West Africa’s desert-adapted herd has survived decades of drought, poaching and instability, but experts say prolonged dry conditions could lead to starvation, dehydration and increased conflict with people as the animals move closer to villages and wells.

Local communities and conservation groups are working to protect remaining water points and reduce tensions between herders and wildlife. But many say the real hope now lies with the skies.

Seasonal rains are expected in June, and conservationists say timely rainfall could replenish water sources and revive vegetation along the elephants’ migration corridor.

Until then, Mali’s desert elephants — symbols of resilience in one of the world’s harshest landscapes — face a perilous wait.
